explanation.body: When the coil is horizontal as shown, its sides cut the magnetic field lines at the greatest rate. The induced e.m.f. therefore has its maximum magnitude.

perOption.B: The output reverses at a zero crossing, when the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field.
perOption.C: The rate of flux cutting varies as the coil turns.
perOption.D: Zero flux linkage here coincides with the greatest rate of change of flux linkage.

difficultyReason: The student must relate the coil’s orientation to the rate of flux cutting.
misconception: Confusing flux with rate of change of flux

explanation.body:
Faraday’s law gives $|\mathcal E|=A|\Delta B|/\Delta t=5.00\pi(8.0\times10^{-2})^2/(10.0\times10^{-3})\approx10.1\ \mathrm V$. Dividing the unrounded e.m.f. by $4.00\ \Omega$ gives $2.51\ \mathrm A$.

By Lenz’s law, the induced field points into the page to oppose the decrease in inward flux. The right-hand grip rule gives a clockwise current.

perOption.B: An anticlockwise current would produce a field out of the page.
perOption.C: The value 10.1 is the e.m.f. in volts, which must be divided by the resistance.
perOption.D: This uses the e.m.f. as the current and gives a field out of the page.

issues: The key prints $B\Delta A/\Delta t$, but its substitution uses the fixed area times the change in flux density. The rewrite uses $A|\Delta B|/\Delta t$ and retains precision until the current is found.
difficultyReason: The student must calculate the e.m.f. and current and apply Lenz’s law to find the direction.
transcription:
A circular coil of diameter $16.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and resistance $4.00\ \Omega$ is placed in a uniform magnetic field of flux density $5.00\ \mathrm{T}$ directed perpendicularly into the coil.

[The diagram shows a circular coil with a horizontal diameter marked $16.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page.]

If the magnetic flux density is reduced to zero at a constant rate over $10.0\ \mathrm{ms}$, what can be deduced about the current flowing in the coil during this change?

Magnitude of current / A | direction
A 2.51 | clockwise
B 2.51 | anticlockwise
C 10.1 | clockwise
D 10.1 | anticlockwise

explanation.body: The turns ratio gives a secondary voltage of $120(10/500)=2.4\ \mathrm V$. The secondary current is $2.4/15=0.16\ \mathrm A$. In an ideal transformer the input and output powers are equal, so $120I_\mathrm p=2.4(0.16)$ and $I_\mathrm p=0.0032\ \mathrm A$.

perOption.C: This uses the numerical value of the secondary voltage as a current.
perOption.D: This applies the primary voltage directly to the secondary resistor.

difficultyReason: The student must link the turns ratio, Ohm’s law and conservation of power.
misconception: Confusing secondary current with primary current
transcription:
A transformer has 500 primary turns and 10 secondary turns. A resistor of $15\ \Omega$ is connected in the secondary coil.

If the root-mean-square voltage across the primary coil is $120\ \mathrm V$, what is the root-mean-square current in the primary coil?

A $0.0032\ \mathrm A$
B $0.16\ \mathrm A$
C $2.4\ \mathrm A$
D $8.0\ \mathrm A$

explanation.body: Diffraction is a wave phenomenon. The fact that electrons produce a diffraction pattern demonstrates their wave nature.

perOption.A: The photoelectric effect demonstrates the particle nature of light.
perOption.B: X-ray diffraction demonstrates the wave nature of X-rays.
perOption.D: Deflection in these fields follows from the electron’s charge and also occurs for classical charged particles.

difficultyReason: The student only needs to recognise diffraction as evidence of wave behaviour.
misconception: Confusing evidence about light with evidence about electrons

explanation.body: The electron and proton have the same charge magnitude, so each gains kinetic energy $E=eV$. Since $E=p^2/(2m)$, the de Broglie wavelength is $\lambda=h/p=h/\sqrt{2mE}$. Thus $\lambda_\mathrm p/\lambda_\mathrm e=\sqrt{m_\mathrm e/m_\mathrm p}=\sqrt{(9.11\times10^{-31})/(1.67\times10^{-27})}=0.0234$.

perOption.A: This uses the electron-to-proton mass ratio without taking its square root.
perOption.C: This takes the reciprocal of the requested wavelength ratio.
perOption.D: This uses the proton-to-electron mass ratio directly.

difficultyReason: The student must connect equal kinetic energies to the inverse square-root dependence on mass.
misconception: Assuming equal kinetic energies imply equal speeds
transcription:
An electron and a proton are accelerated across a potential difference of $15.0\ \mathrm{kV}$.

What is the ratio $\frac{\text{de Broglie wavelength of the proton}}{\text{de Broglie wavelength of the electron}}$?

A $5.45\times10^{-4}$
B $2.34\times10^{-2}$
C $42.8$
D $1.83\times10^3$

explanation.body: The initial count rate from the source alone is $532-24=508$ per minute. After two half-lives it is $508(0.5)^2=127$ per minute. Adding the background gives a detector reading of $127+24=151$ counts per minute.

perOption.A: This gives the remaining source count rate and omits the background.
perOption.B: This quarters the original detector reading, including the background.
perOption.D: This quarters the original reading before adding the background again.

difficultyReason: The arithmetic is simple once the student separates source counts from background counts.
misconception: Applying radioactive decay to the background count
transcription:
A detector of ionising radiation gives a background count rate of 24 per minute.

A radioactive source is placed near the detector and the reading is 532 counts per minute.

What will the reading be after two half-lives of the source?

A 127
B 133
C 151
D 157

explanation.body: The radiation passes through $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ of aluminium, which would stop alpha particles, so the curved track is due to beta radiation. The radius $r=mv/(|q|B)$ is proportional to speed for a given particle in the field. The smaller radius on the left shows that the particle slowed down crossing the sheet from Y to X.

perOption.A: Alpha particles would be stopped by the aluminium, and entry at X would require the particle to speed up in the sheet.
perOption.B: Alpha particles would be stopped by the aluminium.
perOption.C: Entry at X would imply that the particle gained speed in the aluminium.

difficultyReason: The student must use penetration to identify the radiation and curvature to infer its direction of travel.
misconception: Interpreting tighter curvature as higher speed
transcription:
Radiation from a radioactive source enters an evacuated region in which there is a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of the diagram. This region is divided into two by a sheet of aluminium about $1\ \mathrm{mm}$ thick. The curved path followed by the radiation is shown in the figure below.

[A vertical aluminium sheet divides the region. The track between X on the left and Y on the right curves more sharply on the left of the sheet than on the right.]

Which of the following correctly describes the type of radiation and its point of entry?

Type of radiation | point of entry
A alpha | X
B alpha | Y
C beta | X
D beta | Y

explanation.body: Compression does work on the air, and the insulation limits heat transfer. The air gains internal energy and becomes hotter.

perOption.A: The insulation prevents appreciable thermal energy from being supplied to the air.
perOption.C: The rise in air temperature indicates an increase in internal energy.
perOption.D: More frequent collisions do not explain the rise in the molecules’ average kinetic energy.

difficultyReason: The student must recognise that compression transfers energy as work even with negligible heat exchange.
misconception: Treating a temperature rise as proof of heat input

explanation.body: The change in velocity is final minus initial, so $\Delta\mathbf v=\mathbf y-\mathbf x$. With the tails together, the arrow from the tip of $\mathbf x$ to the tip of $\mathbf y$ points down and right.

perOption.A: This reverses the subtraction by pointing from the final tip towards the initial tip.
perOption.C: It points upward even though the upward component falls to zero.
perOption.D: It points left although the rightward velocity component increases.

difficultyReason: The student must subtract the initial velocity vector from the final one using the arrows.
transcription:
The initial velocity of an object is shown by the vector $x$. The final velocity of the object is shown by the vector $y$.

[Vector $x$ points diagonally up and right. Vector $y$ points horizontally to the right and has a greater rightward component than $x$.]

Which arrow best shows the change in velocity of the object?

[A points steeply up and left. B points steeply down and right. C points shallowly up and right. D points shallowly down and left.]

explanation.body: The key selects D because atmospheric pressure alone is about $100\ \mathrm{kPa}$, so the absolute pressure at the pool bottom must be higher. It estimates adult surface area at about $1.9\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and the sprinter’s kinetic energy at $\tfrac12(100)(10)^2=5000\ \mathrm J$. The key uses a domestic air-conditioner estimate of $2500\ \mathrm W$, which over eight hours corresponds to $20\ \mathrm{kWh}$.

perOption.A: As printed, 20 kW is also an unreasonable estimate because the eight-hour calculation gives energy in kWh.
perOption.B: The school’s practical estimate of about 1.9 square metres supports this value.
perOption.C: A 100 kg sprinter at 10 metres per second has this kinetic energy.
perOption.D: Correct. The key assumes absolute pressure.

issues: The printed key picks D and treats pressure as absolute, but A gives 20 kW, whereas 2.5 kW for eight hours gives 20 kWh. D can be a reasonable gauge pressure at a depth of about 1 m. A is the better single choice if D is read as gauge pressure. The question has no unique answer under the key’s absolute-pressure interpretation.
difficultyReason: The student must compare familiar scales and distinguish absolute pressure from gauge pressure.
misconception: Confusing power with energy and absolute pressure with gauge pressure
transcription:
The table below shows the estimates of some physical quantities.

Which row is not a reasonable estimate?

Quantity | value
A power consumption of a domestic aircon turned on for 8 hours | $20\ \mathrm{kW}$
B total surface area of an adult human | $2\ \mathrm{m^2}$
C kinetic energy of an Olympic sprint runner | $5000\ \mathrm J$
D pressure at the bottom of a public swimming pool | $10\ \mathrm{kPa}$

explanation.body: Use $v^2=u^2+2as$ from $y_\mathrm A$ to $y_\mathrm B$, taking upward as positive. Then $(v_\mathrm A/3)^2=v_\mathrm A^2+2(-9.81)(0.40)$, which gives $v_\mathrm A=2.97\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, or $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: This speed is too low to allow the ball to rise 0.40 m, even if it stopped at the higher point.
perOption.B: Adding the squared-speed terms instead of subtracting them gives about 2.7 metres per second.
perOption.D: This is approximately the value of the squared speed before taking its square root.

difficultyReason: The student must substitute the two speeds and the displacement into a constant-acceleration equation.
misconception: Treating the speed ratio as a squared-speed ratio
transcription:
The figure shows the variation of speed $v$ with displacement $y$ of a ball tossed directly upwards. The distance between $y_\mathrm A$ and $y_\mathrm B$ is $0.40\ \mathrm m$. The speed at height $y_\mathrm A$ is $v_\mathrm A$ and the speed at $y_\mathrm B$ is $\frac{v_\mathrm A}{3}$.

[The vertical axis is speed $v$ and the horizontal axis is displacement $y$, with origin marked 0. A decreasing curve passes through $(y_\mathrm A,v_\mathrm A)$ and $(y_\mathrm B,v_\mathrm A/3)$ and reaches zero just beyond $y_\mathrm B$. The interval from $y_\mathrm A$ to $y_\mathrm B$ is labelled $0.40\ \mathrm m$.]

What is speed $v_\mathrm A$?

A $2.6\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
B $2.7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
C $3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$
D $8.9\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$

explanation.body: Let $v$ be the initial speed of X and $V$ the common speed afterwards. Conservation of momentum gives $mv+0=2mV$, so $V=v/2$. The initial kinetic energy is $E_\mathrm k=\tfrac12mv^2$ and the final kinetic energy is $\tfrac12(2m)(v/2)^2=\tfrac14mv^2$. The change is $-\tfrac14mv^2=-E_\mathrm k/2$, so the loss is $E_\mathrm k/2$.

perOption.A: This assumes kinetic energy is conserved when the particles stick together.
perOption.B: This can result from counting only one particle’s final kinetic energy and reporting that value as the loss.
perOption.D: This subtracts the final kinetic energy of only one particle from the initial energy.

difficultyReason: The student must find the common speed using momentum and then use the combined mass in the energy calculation.
misconception: Using one mass for the final kinetic energy
transcription:
A particle X, with kinetic energy $E_\mathrm k$, collides with a stationary particle Y. Both particles have the same mass. After colliding, X and Y travel together as a single larger particle.

How much kinetic energy is lost in the collision?

A $0$
B $\frac{E_\mathrm k}{4}$
C $\frac{E_\mathrm k}{2}$
D $\frac{3E_\mathrm k}{4}$

explanation.body: The acceleration along the slope is $(30-0)/6.0=5.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Resolve the ball’s weight along and perpendicular to the slope. The component along the slope is $mg\sin\theta$, so Newton’s second law gives $mg\sin\theta=5.0m$ and $\theta=\sin^{-1}(5.0/9.81)=30.6^\circ$.

perOption.A: On a level surface the vertical string and the weight provide no horizontal acceleration.
perOption.B: This uses the inverse tangent of the acceleration ratio.
perOption.D: This uses the perpendicular weight component by taking the inverse cosine.

issues: The key prints the acceleration unit as metres per second. The rewrite uses metres per second squared.
difficultyReason: The student must infer that tension has no component along the slope and resolve the weight in that direction.
misconception: Using the acceleration ratio as the tangent of the incline
transcription:
The figure shows a car accelerating down a slope, going from rest to $30\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in $6.0\ \mathrm s$. The slope is angled at $\theta$ above the horizontal.

[The car faces downhill on a slope rising to the right at angle $\theta$. A ball hangs from the ceiling by a string that is tilted by $\theta$ from a dashed vertical line.]

During the acceleration, a ball hangs by a string from the car’s ceiling. The acceleration is such that the string remains perpendicular to the ceiling.

What is the angle $\theta$?

A $0$
B $27^\circ$
C $31^\circ$
D $59^\circ$

explanation.body: Let $W$ be the board’s weight. Taking moments about the hinge before the child steps on gives $2.0F=2.5W$, so $F=1.25W$. With the child on the board, $2.0F'=2.5W+(40)(9.81)(5.0)$, giving $F'=1.25W+981\ \mathrm N$. The extra spring force is $981\ \mathrm N$, so the extra compression is $981/10000=0.0981\ \mathrm m$, or $9.8\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: This is about a factor of ten too small, as when moving the decimal one place too few in the conversion to centimetres.
perOption.B: This reverses the two moment arms, reducing the child’s weight by a factor of 2.0/5.0.
perOption.D: This overestimates the extra spring force, which is fixed by the child’s moment about the hinge.

difficultyReason: The student must isolate the extra spring force using moments and convert it to compression with Hooke’s law.
transcription:
A diving board of length $5.0\ \mathrm m$ is hinged at one end and supported $2.0\ \mathrm m$ from this end by a spring of spring constant $10\ \mathrm{kN\,m^{-1}}$. A child of mass $40\ \mathrm{kg}$ stands at the far end of the board.

[The hinge is at the right end of the horizontal diving board. The spring supports the board $2.0\ \mathrm m$ to the left of the hinge, and the child stands $5.0\ \mathrm m$ from the hinge at the left end.]

What is the extra compression of the spring caused by the child standing on the end of the board?

A $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$
B $1.6\ \mathrm{cm}$
C $9.8\ \mathrm{cm}$
D $16\ \mathrm{cm}$

explanation.body: The spring’s elastic energy increases by $\tfrac12(181)(0.036^2-0.021^2)=0.07738\ \mathrm J$. The mass loses gravitational potential energy of $3.8(0.178-0.163)=0.057\ \mathrm J$. Subtracting this energy supplied by gravity gives the work done by $F$, $0.07738-0.057=0.0204\ \mathrm J$.

perOption.A: This is the work done by gravity alone.
perOption.C: This gives the increase in elastic potential energy without subtracting the loss of gravitational potential energy.
perOption.D: This adds the loss of gravitational potential energy instead of subtracting it.

difficultyReason: The student must subtract gravity’s work from the increase in elastic energy using the initial and final extensions.
misconception: Attributing all the gain in elastic energy to the added force
transcription:
A mass of weight $3.8\ \mathrm N$ is suspended on a spring of unstretched length $14.2\ \mathrm{cm}$ and spring constant $181\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. The length of the spring is $16.3\ \mathrm{cm}$ as shown in (a).

An additional force $F$ then extends the spring so that its length becomes $17.8\ \mathrm{cm}$ as shown in (b).

[(a) A spring hangs from a fixed point and is $16.3\ \mathrm{cm}$ long, with a downward arrow of $3.8\ \mathrm N$ on the mass. (b) The spring hangs from a fixed point and is $17.8\ \mathrm{cm}$ long, with downward arrows $F$ and $3.8\ \mathrm N$ on the mass.]

What is the work done by $F$?

A $0.057\ \mathrm J$
B $0.020\ \mathrm J$
C $0.077\ \mathrm J$
D $0.13\ \mathrm J$
